title: Assistant handbook mini PRD draft
body:
Goal:
- Small, composable feature to let customers attach a lightweight 'handbook' to a model route: curated style guides, allowed/disallowed phrases, response templates, example snippets, and metadata that help keep assistant behavior consistent across apps and deployments.

Problem summary:
- customers struggle with drift across prompts, teams ship ad-hoc system messages, compliance wants auditable behavior presets, and PMs want a simple way to standardize tone/format without reinventing prompts in every client.

Hypothesis:
- If we provide a first-class handbook that is versioned and served alongside a route, teams will ship fewer ad-hoc system messages, reduce regressions in tone/format, and accelerate audits.

Primary personas:
- platform devs: want API to attach handbook and roll forward/back versions.
- product managers: want UI to author templates and quick previews.
- compliance/security: need simple policy snippets and an audit trail.
- integrators (SEs): want examples and quick toggles to A/B test.

User stories (MVP):
- as a dev, I can attach handbook v1.0 to a route via API and see preview of system message merge.
- as a PM, I can author a one-page handbook that includes tone, 3 canned response templates, and a list of banned topics.
- as a compliance officer, I can view handbook change history and export diffs for audits.
- as an operator, I can configure 'suggest' vs 'enforce' behavior per handbook.

MVP features (rough):
- JSON/YAML handbook schema: metadata, tone, 0..N templates, policy snippets, example prompts, transform hints (truncate/prefix).
- Console editor: simple fields + live model preview using chosen model.
- API endpoints: create/list/get/attach/activate handbook versions.
- Versioning + rollback UI.
- Telemetry hooks: which handbook applied, acceptance rate, deviations (model ignoring instructions).

Non-goals for MVP:
- full policy enforcement (no runtime content blocking in first pass).
- complex natural language reconciliation engines.

Technical notes / considerations:
- handbook served as route metadata; runtime merges handbook into system message order before request.
- offer 'strength' flag: preference|soft|hard. Soft = include as system message but still allow override; hard = prepend and mark for telemetry.
- fallback: if handbook incompatible with model (token limit), we send compacted handbook via prefix compression or reference ID and fall back to default system message.
- storage: small objects in config DB, immutable versions.
- evaluation: add synthetic prompt set to measure compliance and tone drift on deployment.

Open questions / risks:
- how to measure when model 'ignores' handbook? heuristics vs human eval.
- policy snippets might create compliance liability if misused. Need guardrails.
- interactions with function-calling and streaming: should handbook influence function outputs? probably yes, but needs explicit rules.
- UX: do we show handbook to end-users (transparency) or keep internal only?

Quick UI sketch (notes to self):
- left: list of handbook versions, create button.
- center: editor with fields: name, summary, tone selector (formal/friendly/concise), templates list, banned-terms list, example Q/A.
- right: live preview + test prompt input, acceptance score and warnings.

Metrics to track:
- adoption: % of routes with handbook attached.
- compliance delta: rate of policy violations pre/post.
- deviation rate: % of responses that diverge from templates by beyond threshold.
- ops: rollback events and time-to-rollback.

Next steps / TODOs:
- quick spike: prototype handbook schema + runtime merge in sandbox. (ENG spike: 1 week).
- design: 2 mocks for console editor and preview.
- evaluation: define 10 canonical prompts for synthetic compliance tests.
- sync with legal to align policy snippet guidance.

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- could be an extension of route metadata rather than separate object, but versions are cleaner.
- long term: public library of community handbooks and templates.
- consider 'handbook inheritance' (org-level defaults with route-level overrides).
- think about size limits and cost of sending big handbooks to low-latency routes.

End of note.
